<reason>High-quality, genuinely contested debate. Side A built a sophisticated necessity/proportionality framework and landed the best single counter: defusing PRO's irreversibility trump by showing targeted browsing control can protect regeneration now, so "compensation is revisable, degradation is not" does not resolve the method choice. But Side B controlled the decisive terrain. Its unique-mechanism argument (predators restore self-regulation; CON's alternative is perpetual, publicly funded culls—"a subscription to standing still") was never refuted, only demoted by A's assertion that self-regulation is "not a trump card." B's Q1 forced A to specify a certifier and concede Yellowstone would pass despite organized opposition, which B converted into a strong closing convergence move, while A's answer that "feasibility is not necessity" only partly recovered because B had in fact offered a complete whole-policy comparison. B also engaged A's cost critique honestly (conceding continuing costs while defending a front-loaded, declining trajectory) and gave direct, complete answers to both pressure questions, whereas A's answer to the mechanism question was a partial reframe. A's cooperation/hollow-consultation point survived unanswered, keeping this competitive, but B's clearer decision rule, stronger comparative case, and more damaging pressure sequence give PRO the cleaner path on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive sequence was B's Rebuttal 1 "a delay with no endpoint... is the veto in slow motion," sharpened by Q1 demanding a certifier and one real-world case passing A's test; A's Yellowstone concession in Rebuttal 2 plugged the hole but let B close with "that is our plan... Yellowstone is proof the mechanism works." A's closing rebuttal (the concession answers whether override is possible, not what justifies it) was the strongest counter-move and kept the margin to clear-but-competitive rather than dominant.</best_rebuttal>
